tips.title: Sparrenburg
tips.text: A 13th-century castle on the ridge above the old town, built by the Counts of Ravensberg.
tips.more: Its tower looks out over the city and the Teutoburg Forest. Below the walls, old passages run through the hill.

tips.title: Kunsthalle Bielefeld
tips.text: The American architect Philip Johnson designed this red sandstone museum, opened in 1968.
tips.more: Johnson, famous for his Glass House in Connecticut, built very little in Europe. The Kunsthalle shows modern and contemporary art, with sculptures in the park beside it.

tips.title: Externsteine
tips.text: Sandstone pillars rising out of the Teutoburg Forest, with a relief carved into the rock almost 900 years ago.
tips.more: Steps and a small chapel are cut into the rock, and a bridge links two of the pillars. A good outing from Bielefeld.

tips.title: Berlin Wall Memorial
tips.text: The last stretch of the Wall with its death strip intact, along Bernauer Strasse.
tips.more: The houses on this street stood right on the border, and in 1961 people jumped from their windows to the West. A viewing tower looks over the preserved border strip.

tips.title: Einstein Tower
tips.text: An observatory built around 1920 to test Albert Einstein’s theory of relativity.
tips.more: Erich Mendelsohn’s curved tower on the Telegrafenberg in Potsdam became an icon of expressionist architecture. It still holds a solar telescope.

tips.title: Tempelhofer Feld
tips.text: An airport in the middle of the city that closed in 2008; its runways are now a park for everyone.
tips.more: People cycle, skate and fly kites on the old runways. During the Berlin Airlift of 1948–49 the planes supplying West Berlin landed here.

tips.title: Elbphilharmonie
tips.text: A concert hall rising like a glass wave out of an old brick warehouse in the harbour.
tips.more: Its public viewing platform, the Plaza, sits 37 metres up between the old warehouse and the new glass building and is open to everyone.

tips.title: Beatles-Platz
tips.text: Before they were famous, the Beatles played hundreds of nights in the clubs of the Grosse Freiheit, right here.
tips.more: Between 1960 and 1962 they performed at the Indra, the Kaiserkeller, the Top Ten and the Star-Club. The round square at the corner of the Reeperbahn remembers them with steel figures.

tips.title: Old Elbe Tunnel
tips.text: Lifts big enough for cars take you 24 metres down to a tiled tunnel under the Elbe, opened in 1911.
tips.more: Walk through it to the other bank and look back at the harbour and the Landungsbrücken.

tips.title: Viktualienmarkt
tips.text: Munich’s open-air food market since 1807, with a maypole in the middle and a beer garden.
tips.more: Stalls sell fruit, cheese, flowers and Bavarian specialities a few steps from Marienplatz.

tips.title: Lenbachhaus
tips.text: This villa museum holds the largest collection of the Blue Rider, the artists around Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc.
tips.more: Many of the works were a gift from Gabriele Münter, who hid them from the Nazis in her house in Murnau and gave them to the city in 1957.

tips.title: Olympiapark
tips.text: The park of the 1972 Olympic Games, with transparent tent roofs and a hill made of wartime rubble.
tips.more: From the top of the Olympiaberg the view reaches the Alps on clear days.

tips.title: Cologne Cathedral
tips.text: Building began in 1248 and was only finished in 1880; for a few years it was the tallest building in the world.
tips.more: 533 steps lead up the south tower to a view over the Rhine. Inside stands the golden Shrine of the Three Kings.

tips.title: Museum Ludwig
tips.text: Right next to the cathedral, one of the largest collections of Pop Art outside the United States.
tips.more: It also holds one of the biggest Picasso collections in Europe.

tips.title: Hohenzollern Bridge
tips.text: Tens of thousands of love locks hang on the railway bridge leading to the cathedral.
tips.more: Couples have fastened padlocks to its fence since about 2008. Over 1,000 trains a day cross the bridge.

tips.title: Römer
tips.text: The old town square with its half-timbered houses and the Römer, the city hall since 1405.
tips.more: Emperors were celebrated here after their coronation. Most of the houses were rebuilt after the Second World War.

tips.title: Goethe House
tips.text: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was born in this house in 1749 and wrote his first works here.
tips.more: The house was destroyed in 1944 and rebuilt; much of the original furniture had been saved and is back in its place.

tips.title: Main Tower
tips.text: Frankfurt’s only skyscraper with a viewing platform open to the public, about 200 metres up.
tips.more: From the top you look out over the towers of the banks, the river Main and the Taunus hills.

tips.title: St. Nicholas Church
tips.text: The Monday prayers for peace in this church grew into the demonstrations of autumn 1989.
tips.more: On 9 October 1989, some 70,000 people marched peacefully around the city ring, a turning point on the way to the fall of the Wall.

tips.title: St. Thomas Church
tips.text: Johann Sebastian Bach was cantor here for 27 years and is buried in front of the altar.
tips.more: The St. Thomas Boys Choir, which Bach led, still sings here every week.

tips.title: Monument to the Battle of the Nations
tips.wiki: Monument to the Battle of the Nations
tips.text: A 91-metre stone monument to the battle of 1813 against Napoleon, finished in 1913.
tips.more: Inside, giant stone figures guard a crypt, and the platform at the top looks out over the whole city.

tips.title: Frauenkirche
tips.text: Destroyed in 1945, its ruins were a memorial for decades; it was rebuilt from 1994 and consecrated again in 2005.
tips.more: Many of the old stones were put back in their original places; they show up darker in the new walls.

tips.title: Blue Wonder
tips.text: A blue steel bridge across the Elbe from 1893 that the people of Dresden call the Blue Wonder.
tips.more: Next to it, one of the oldest suspension railways in the world climbs the hillside.

tips.title: Beethoven House
tips.text: Ludwig van Beethoven was born in this house in 1770.
tips.more: It holds the largest Beethoven collection in the world, among it his last grand piano and his ear trumpets.

tips.title: Musée d’Orsay
tips.text: A grand railway station from 1900 that now holds the world’s best-known collection of Impressionist paintings.
tips.more: Look for the huge station clocks; through the glass of one of them you see across the Seine to the Louvre and Montmartre.

tips.title: Shakespeare and Company
tips.text: An English-language bookshop by the Seine where young writers may sleep among the shelves.
tips.more: George Whitman opened it in 1951 and named it after Sylvia Beach’s shop of the 1920s, which first published James Joyce’s Ulysses.

tips.title: Catacombs of Paris
tips.text: Below the streets lie the bones of some six million Parisians, moved here from overflowing cemeteries from the 1780s on.
tips.more: A walk of about 1.5 km leads through old quarry tunnels lined with stacked bones.

tips.title: Borough Market
tips.text: One of London’s oldest food markets, trading by London Bridge for many centuries.
tips.more: Under its Victorian iron roofs you find cheese, bread, game and street food from all over the world.

tips.title: Charles Dickens Museum
tips.text: Charles Dickens lived in this terraced house when he wrote Oliver Twist.
tips.more: He moved in with his young family in 1837. Rooms are furnished as in his day, with his writing desk.

tips.title: Royal Observatory, Greenwich
tips.text: Stand with one foot in each hemisphere on the prime meridian, longitude 0°.
tips.more: All time zones of the world were once counted from here, Greenwich Mean Time. The red time ball on the roof still drops at 1 pm.

tips.title: Pantheon
tips.text: A temple almost 1,900 years old whose dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
tips.more: Light and rain fall through the open eye at the top, the oculus; small holes in the floor drain the water.

tips.title: Keats-Shelley House
tips.text: The English poet John Keats died in a room of this house at the Spanish Steps in 1821, aged 25.
tips.more: Today it is a museum of the English Romantic poets who loved Rome, among them Keats, Shelley and Byron.

tips.title: Mouth of Truth
tips.text: A marble face said to bite off the hand of anyone who tells a lie.
tips.more: The ancient disc, probably once a drain cover, hangs in the porch of the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

tips.title: La Boqueria
tips.text: A covered market off La Rambla, with stalls of fruit, ham and seafood.
tips.more: Small bars inside the market cook what is sold around them.

tips.title: Sagrada Família
tips.text: Antoni Gaudí worked on this basilica for over 40 years and is buried in its crypt; building goes on to this day.
tips.more: Gaudí designed its columns like trees, so the light inside falls as in a forest.

tips.title: Montserrat
tips.text: A saw-toothed mountain with a monastery on its side, about an hour from the city.
tips.more: A rack railway and a cable car climb to the monastery, home of the Black Madonna and one of Europe’s oldest boys’ choirs.

tips.title: Belém Tower
tips.text: A 16th-century fortress on the Tagus that guarded the way in and out of the harbour in the Age of Discovery.
tips.more: Its stonework shows ropes, armillary spheres and a carved rhinoceros.

tips.title: A Brasileira
tips.text: The poet Fernando Pessoa was a regular at this café, opened in 1905; his bronze figure sits at a table outside.
tips.more: Order a bica, the small Lisbon espresso, and take the seat next to him.

tips.title: Pena Palace
tips.text: A brightly painted 19th-century palace on a hilltop in the forests of Sintra.
tips.more: On clear days you can see from its terraces to Lisbon and the Atlantic.

tips.title: Rijksmuseum
tips.text: The national museum of the Netherlands, home of Rembrandt’s Night Watch; a cycle path runs right through the building.
tips.more: Over 8,000 objects tell 800 years of Dutch art and history.

tips.title: Anne Frank House
tips.text: Anne Frank hid with her family in the secret annex of this canal house for two years and wrote her diary here.
tips.more: The bookcase that hid the entrance is still in place.

tips.title: Zaanse Schans
tips.text: Working windmills and green wooden houses by the river Zaan, about 15 km from the centre.
tips.more: Some of the mills still grind spices and press oil as they did 300 years ago.

tips.title: Naschmarkt
tips.text: Vienna’s best-known market, about 1.5 km of stalls along the Wienzeile.
tips.more: On Saturdays a flea market joins it at the far end.

tips.title: Mozarthaus
tips.text: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart lived in this apartment from 1784 to 1787 and wrote The Marriage of Figaro here.
tips.more: It is the only one of his Vienna homes that still stands.

tips.title: Wiener Riesenrad
tips.text: One of the oldest Ferris wheels still turning, built in 1897 in the Prater.
tips.more: Its red cabins rise to almost 65 metres above the amusement park.

tips.title: Charles Bridge
tips.text: A stone bridge from the 14th century lined with 30 statues of saints.
tips.more: Early in the morning, before the crowds arrive, it belongs to the photographers.

tips.title: Golden Lane
tips.text: Franz Kafka wrote in the little blue house at number 22 of this lane of tiny castle houses.
tips.more: He used it as a quiet place to write in 1916 and 1917, staying into the night.

tips.title: Sedlec Ossuary
tips.text: A chapel decorated with the bones of tens of thousands of people, in the town of Kutná Hora.
tips.more: Even the chandelier is made of bones. Kutná Hora is about an hour from Prague by train.

tips.title: Hagia Sophia
tips.text: Built as a church in 537, it became a mosque in 1453; its dome has shaped the city for almost 1,500 years.
tips.more: Christian mosaics and Islamic calligraphy are seen side by side inside.

tips.title: Museum of Innocence
tips.text: Nobel laureate Orhan Pamuk wrote a novel and built this museum of everyday objects to go with it.
tips.more: Each display case belongs to a chapter of the book, and a ticket is printed inside the novel.

tips.title: Basilica Cistern
tips.text: An underground water tank from the 6th century, held up by 336 columns; two of them rest on Medusa heads.
tips.more: It once stored water for the Great Palace of the Byzantine emperors.

tips.title: High Line
tips.text: An old elevated freight railway on Manhattan’s West Side turned into a park in the air.
tips.more: The walk runs about 2.3 km above the streets, with plants that grew wild on the tracks.

tips.title: Louis Armstrong House
tips.text: Louis Armstrong lived in this modest house in Queens from 1943 until his death in 1971.
tips.more: He could have lived anywhere, but chose to stay among his neighbours; his home recordings are played in the rooms.

tips.title: Grand Central Terminal
tips.text: Whisper into a corner of the tiled arches outside the Oyster Bar, and someone in the far corner hears you.
tips.more: Look up in the main hall: the ceiling shows the constellations, painted in reverse.

tips.title: Alcatraz Island
tips.text: The island prison in the bay, closed in 1963, once held Al Capone.
tips.more: Ferries leave from Pier 33; the audio tour is told by former guards and inmates.

tips.title: City Lights Bookstore
tips.text: Poet Lawrence Ferlinghetti’s bookshop published Allen Ginsberg’s Howl in 1956 and became the home of the Beat writers.
tips.more: The poetry room upstairs invites you to sit down and read.

tips.title: Cable cars
tips.text: The last cable cars in the world still worked by hand, running since 1873.
tips.more: At the end of the line on Powell Street the cars are turned around on a turntable, pushed by the crew.

tips.title: Palacio de Bellas Artes
tips.text: A white marble palace of the arts, with murals by Diego Rivera inside.
tips.more: Its stage curtain is made of nearly a million pieces of coloured glass by Tiffany.

tips.title: Frida Kahlo Museum
tips.text: Frida Kahlo was born, lived and died in this blue house in Coyoacán.
tips.more: Her studio, her easel and her clothes are still in the house, which she shared with Diego Rivera.

tips.title: Xochimilco
tips.text: Colourful boats glide along canals that are a remnant of the old Aztec lake landscape.
tips.more: Mariachi bands and food sellers pull up alongside in their own boats.

tips.title: Christ the Redeemer
tips.text: The 30-metre statue on Corcovado mountain, 700 metres above the city.
tips.more: A rack railway through the Tijuca forest climbs to its feet.

tips.title: Selarón Steps
tips.text: Chilean artist Jorge Selarón covered these 215 steps with tiles from all over the world.
tips.more: He worked on them for more than 20 years; visitors sent him tiles from their home countries.

tips.title: Sugarloaf Mountain
tips.text: Two cable cars climb via Urca hill to the top of the granite peak at the mouth of the bay.
tips.more: Come for the sunset over the city and Copacabana.

tips.title: Caminito
tips.text: A colourful street in La Boca, painted like the houses of the dock workers who settled here.
tips.more: Tango dancers perform on the pavement for passers-by.

tips.title: Café Tortoni
tips.text: The city’s oldest café, opened in 1858, where Jorge Luis Borges and Carlos Gardel were guests.
tips.more: Tango shows still take place in its cellar.

tips.title: Recoleta Cemetery
tips.text: A city of marble mausoleums where Eva Perón is buried.
tips.more: Its avenues and statues make it one of the most visited cemeteries in the world.

tips.title: Khan el-Khalili
tips.text: A bazaar of narrow lanes founded in the 14th century in the heart of old Cairo.
tips.more: Stop at one of the old coffee houses for mint tea.

tips.title: Pyramids of Giza
tips.text: The last of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, right at the edge of the city.
tips.more: The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure built by people for more than 3,800 years.

tips.title: Table Mountain
tips.text: The flat-topped mountain above the city, reached by a cable car whose floor turns as it climbs.
tips.more: When clouds pour over its edge, people here say the table cloth is laid.

tips.title: Robben Island
tips.text: Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison on this island.
tips.more: Tours are led by former political prisoners and stop at his cell.

tips.title: Boulders Beach
tips.text: African penguins nest on this beach between granite boulders.
tips.more: Wooden walkways lead you right past the colony.

tips.title: Nairobi National Museum
tips.text: Kenya’s national museum, with collections on the country’s history, nature, culture and art.
tips.more: A snake park is part of the museum grounds.

tips.title: Nairobi National Park
tips.text: Lions, rhinos and giraffes live in a national park with the city skyline in the background.
tips.more: It lies only about 7 km from the centre of the capital.

tips.title: Sensō-ji
tips.text: Tokyo’s oldest temple, reached through the Thunder Gate with its giant red lantern.
tips.more: The shopping street in front of it has sold snacks and souvenirs to pilgrims for centuries.

tips.title: Ghibli Museum
tips.text: Hayao Miyazaki designed this museum of the Studio Ghibli films himself; a robot soldier guards its roof garden.
tips.more: Tickets name a date and time and are sold in advance only.

tips.title: Shibuya Crossing
tips.text: When the lights turn green, crowds cross this junction from all sides at once.
tips.more: The statue of the faithful dog Hachikō waits by the station exit.

tips.title: Kinkaku-ji
tips.text: A Zen temple whose top two floors are covered in gold leaf.
tips.more: It is mirrored in the pond in front of it.

tips.title: Fushimi Inari-taisha
tips.text: Thousands of vermilion torii gates form tunnels up a wooded mountain.
tips.more: Each gate was given by a person or a company; the walk to the top takes about two hours.

tips.title: Gyeongbokgung
tips.text: The main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, first built in 1395.
tips.more: The changing of the guard takes place at its main gate.

tips.title: Gwangjang Market
tips.text: One of Korea’s oldest markets, famous for its mung bean pancakes.
tips.more: Hundreds of food stalls fill the covered lanes.

tips.title: Cheonggyecheon
tips.text: A stream once buried under an elevated highway flows through the city centre again.
tips.more: The highway was torn down and the stream opened up in 2005; it is now an almost 11 km walk.

tips.title: Forbidden City
tips.text: The palace of 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties.
tips.more: For almost 500 years no one could enter without the emperor’s permission.

tips.title: Temple of Heaven
tips.text: Emperors prayed here for good harvests, in a round hall of wood under a blue roof.
tips.more: Today the park is full of people doing tai chi, dancing and playing cards in the mornings.

tips.title: Mutianyu
tips.text: A restored stretch of the Great Wall about 70 km from the city.
tips.more: A chairlift goes up and a toboggan run brings you back down.

tips.title: Gardens by the Bay
tips.text: Steel Supertrees up to 50 metres tall, planted with ferns and orchids.
tips.more: Every evening they light up to music.

tips.title: Lau Pa Sat
tips.text: A Victorian cast-iron market hall that is now a busy food centre.
tips.more: At night the street beside it fills with satay stalls.

tips.title: Pulau Ubin
tips.text: An island of village houses and mangroves, a short boat ride from the mainland.
tips.more: Rent a bicycle and explore one of the last kampongs, traditional villages, of Singapore.

tips.title: Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus
tips.text: A Victorian Gothic railway station, still one of the busiest in India.
tips.more: It was finished in 1888 and is a World Heritage Site.

tips.title: Mani Bhavan
tips.text: Mahatma Gandhi stayed in this house whenever he was in Bombay from 1917 to 1934.
tips.more: His room, with his spinning wheel, is kept as it was.

tips.title: Elephanta Caves
tips.text: Rock-cut temples with a huge three-headed Shiva, on an island in the harbour.
tips.more: Ferries leave from the Gateway of India.

tips.title: Sydney Opera House
tips.text: Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the design competition in 1957, but left in 1966 and never saw the finished building.
tips.more: The roof shells are covered with more than a million tiles.

tips.title: Sydney Harbour Bridge
tips.text: You can climb the arch of the bridge, 134 metres above the harbour.
tips.more: Locals call it the Coathanger.

tips.title: Bondi Beach
tips.text: Australia’s best-known beach, with an ocean pool cut into the rocks at its southern end.
tips.more: A coastal path leads along the cliffs to Coogee.

tips.title: Acropolis
tips.text: The Parthenon has stood on this rock above the city for almost 2,500 years.
tips.more: The Acropolis Museum at its foot shows the sculptures that once decorated the temples.

tips.title: Ancient Agora
tips.text: Socrates questioned the citizens of Athens in this marketplace.
tips.more: The Temple of Hephaestus above the agora is one of the best preserved Greek temples.

tips.title: Cape Sounion
tips.text: The ruins of a temple of Poseidon on a cape above the Aegean, about 70 km from Athens.
tips.more: Lord Byron carved his name into one of its columns.

tips.title: Vasa Museum
tips.text: A warship that sank on its maiden voyage in 1628 and was raised almost intact in 1961.
tips.more: It is the best preserved ship of its time anywhere.

tips.title: ABBA The Museum
tips.text: The story of the band that won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1974 with Waterloo.
tips.more: Costumes, gold records and a copy of the studio where many of the songs were recorded.

tips.title: Metro art
tips.text: Over 90 of the 100 metro stations are decorated with art; some look like painted caves.
tips.more: Start at T-Centralen, with its blue vines on the rock walls.
